text_blocks.snippet: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes high blood pressure in the lung arteries, which strains the right side of the heart.
In the early stages, PAH often causes no symptoms or mimics other heart and lung conditions. As it progresses, the most frequent signs include:

list.snippet: Shortness of breath (dyspnea), especially during physical activity or exertion
Fatigue and unusual tiredness during daily tasks
Chest pain, pressure, or discomfort resulting from an overworked heart
Dizziness or lightheadedness, particularly when moving or exerting yourself
Heart palpitations (a racing or pounding heartbeat)

text_blocks.snippet: As right-sided heart strain or failure develops, more pronounced physical signs may appear:

list.snippet: Swelling (edema) in the ankles, feet, legs, or abdomen due to fluid retention
Fainting spells (syncope) triggered by reduced oxygen flow to the brain
Bluish lips or skin (cyanosis) caused by low blood oxygen levels
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) or hoarseness from an enlarged artery pressing on chest nerves in rare, severe cases

text_blocks.snippet: For a detailed overview of the condition and diagnostic steps, visit the American Lung Association Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension Guide.
